World.title: ‘He’s not a cheater’: DeChambeau to continue playing at British Open as controversy erupts over two-shot penalty
World.content:
Updated SportGolfBritish Open ‘He’s not a cheater’: DeChambeau to continue playing at British Open as controversy erupts over two-shot penalty Tom Decent Updated July 18, 2026 — 10:13am ,first published July 18, 2026 — 8:07am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Southport: Controversy has erupted at the British Open, with American star Bryson DeChambeau set to continue his campaign after initially threatening to withdraw from the tournament when he was controversially docked two shots by officials on Friday. DeChambeau was hit with a two-shot penalty for “improving the area” of his intended back swing during his second round, prompting his agent to declare his client wasn’t a cheat and he wasn’t trying to gain an unfair advantage during an incident that has divided the golf world. Bryson DeChambeau speaks with officials after his round on Friday at the British Open. X After carding a four-under 66 on Friday, DeChambeau walked off the 18th green at Royal Birkdale in outright second on seven-under, behind Australia’s Lucas Herbert, who shot a record-equalling 62 to head to the weekend at eight-under. But after signing his card, DeChambeau was approached by rules officials over an incident on the fifth hole earlier in the day.



Playing his second shot from thick rough, television footage appeared to show DeChambeau walking around the area of his ball before taking his shot, with officials believing his actions improved the area where his club would swing. Although the ball itself never moved, the rules of golf prohibit players from improving the area of an intended stance or swing, even if the action is accidental. DeChambeau and his agent Brett Falkoff (left) on a controversial evening at the British Open. Getty Images A frustrated DeChambeau was taken back to the fifth hole by officials, where he remonstrated with tournament staff and appeared to tell decision-makers he would not continue in the championship. His manager was also present during the dramatic exchange broadcast on live television. Shortly afterwards, amid a crush of television cameras and reporters, tournament rules official Grant Moir confirmed DeChambeau had been docked two shots. His bogey on the 5th hole would become a triple bogey seven.



The penalty dropped DeChambeau from seven-under to five-under, leaving him tied for fifth rather than second. “Bryson has been penalised two strokes for inadvertently improving the area of intended back swing on fifth hole,” Moir said. Grant Moir, executive director of governance at The R&A, speaks to the media regarding a two-stoke penalty assessed against DeChambeau. Getty Images “Ruling one restricts what a player may do to improve any of the protected conditions affecting the stroke and this includes the area of the player’s intended swing. “So an improvement means to alter one or more of the conditions affecting the stroke so that the player gains a potential advantage for the stroke. Now, I’ll stress that this applies even when the action is accidental, as it was in Bryson’s case.”



When asked by reporters as he walked away whether he would return for Saturday’s third round, DeChambeau stopped short of giving any assurance. DeChambeau’s agent Brett Falkoff also said he would decide on Saturday morning whether he would continue playing but said his 32-year-old client is angry. However, at 12.02am UK time, DeChambeau wrote on X: “Obviously disappointed with the ruling. I don’t agree with it, but it is what it is. This fires me up. Onto the weekend. Let’s get it.” Earlier, DeChambeau headed to the practice range after being informed of his penalty, where he began hitting balls as darkness fell over Royal Birkdale. “He’s a lot of things. He’s not a cheater,” Falkoff said. “He’s a big boy … but he certainly feels he was unfairly penalised.”



Related Article British Open Herbert stuns with record-equalling round at British Open, but final putt could haunt him forever DeChambeau is a popular player on tour but also divisive among fans, having defected to LIV Golf on a lucrative deal worth more than $100 million (USD). Herbert was supposed to be paired with DeChambeau on Saturday but the latest drama means he will instead play his third round with Jackson Suber at 3.50pm local time (12.50am AEST). DeChambeau, a two-time US Open champion, is listed to tee off at 3.30pm (12.30am). He has never won a British Open. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: With a beloved children’s author on the bill, this Perth festival isn’t afraid to sort fact from fiction
World.content:
NationalWACity life With a beloved children’s author on the bill, this Perth festival isn’t afraid to sort fact from fiction Cameron Myles July 18, 2026 — 10:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It has been a turbulent time for writers’ festivals over the past few years. In South Australia, the controversy with the Adelaide Writers’ Week boycotts and eventual cancellation are well documented. In Bendigo last year, dozens of authors quit the writers’ festival, leading to the cancellation of the opening night gala. Children’s author Mem Fox will be at this year’s Festival of Fiction. Meanwhile, in WA, it was announced in 2024 that the Perth Writers Weekend was to move to a standalone event to be held in spring 2026, having previously been part of the Perth Festival. It is against this cultural backdrop that another festival returns to Perth’s literary scene this year, with its focus remaining firmly on the fiction aisles.



Perth’s Festival of Fiction has announced its line-up for 2026, with names on the billing including beloved children’s author Mem Fox, award-winning writer Christos Tsiolkas, alongside the likes of Sally Hepworth and Kate Morton. Christos Tsiolkas has taken the tired ploy of the self-referential text and reinvigorated it. Eddie Jim Festival director Tess Woods said the appeal of festivals was clear – they offered a reprieve, an ability to get out and engage with those who write the books we love, or even loathe. “We’re getting more and more divisive, and we’re seeing that you know across social media and in politics,” she said. “And there’s very little nuance left now on both sides of the spectrum.



“So festivals are an opportunity for us to see each other face-to-face, to get away from our keyboards, and to see that, you know, maybe an author whose political opinion you don’t agree with, you see them on stage and you’re like, ‘You know this is a human, this is a person with feelings, who laughs and who has a family’.” Related Article Literature Adelaide Festival attendance halved in wake of Writers’ Week drama The benefit extends beyond the experience of readers. Writers, Woods notes, spend a lot of time by themselves, and festivals are a good way to meet others and expand their networks. For Woods, who will finish up as director after this year’s festival, the prioritising of fiction was both a much-needed point of difference and a drawcard. “I felt that genre fiction writers were often excluded from the more traditional mainstream literary festivals,” she said.



“They throw them a bone. You would have, your two or three crime writers, or your two or three, general fiction writers, and then they were mostly dominated by literary fiction, poets, non-fiction, journalists, memoir [writers]. “And so I felt that the books that you’re seeing in Big W and Dymocks that are making up that top 10, that are keeping the publishing industry alive, that your average punter is going out to buy - your crime and your romance and fantasy - they just weren’t represented enough at the big literary festivals.” The festival has two Miles Franklin award-winners on the billing – Siang Lu and Sofie Laguna – as well as Toni Jordan, who was longlisted for the prestigious award. And Fox, the author of Australian children’s classics such as Possum Magic, Time for Bed, and Where is the Green Sheep will be holding workshops on something she is no doubt an expert in – “how to find the right words”. While major challenges revolving around freedom of speech and politics made headlines, Woods said the ever-present threat to writers’ festivals was funding.



“We have run this festival three years now with a committee of 20 volunteers, unpaid, and it’s just been a labor of love,” she said. “We’re very lucky that the City of Joondalup have generously sponsored us, so we’ve got that Joondalup funding, but it’s just not enough to make it keep going. “For the last two years, we haven’t had a Perth Writers Festival. I think we’re the only state in Australia after Adelaide had theirs canceled that hasn’t got one.” The Festival of Fiction will return to Edith Cowan University’s Joondalup campus on November 21-22.

World.title: Ronnie Di Stasio on closing the pioneering Cafe Di Stasio after 38 years
World.content:
As the sun sets on one of Melbourne’s most influential Italian restaurants, its creator and his partner Mallory Wall remember the chaos, the hard times and St Kilda of old.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Restaurateur Rinaldo Di Stasio pulled an all-nighter on Tuesday as champagne-fuelled celebrations for the sale of Cafe Di Stasio morphed into a 5am World Cup watch party. His St Kilda hive of Italian good times this week passed into the hands of one of its former chefs, Nathan Presley, who will reopen it in August as a seafood restaurant. After 38 years, the Campari-soaked reign of 71-year-old Di Stasio over the Fitzroy Street dining room that helped propel Melbourne’s restaurant scene onto the global stage is over. 1 / 11 Regulars loved the restaurant's hedonistic atmosphere as much as its food. Courtesy Rinaldo Di Stasio and Mallory Wall 2 / 11 Rinaldo Di Stasio at the St Kilda restaurant in 1991. Mario Borg 3 / 11 Cafe Di Stasio in St Kilda circa 2012. Supplied 4 / 11 Rinaldo Di Stasio built a reputation for long lunches and late nights at Cafe Di Stasio. Courtesy Rinaldo Di Stasio and Mallory Wall 5 / 11 Old s for Cafe Di Stasio. Courtesy Rinaldo Di Stasio and Mallory Wall 6 / 11 One  shows Rinaldo Di Stasio with shirtless waiter Benito Rega. Courtesy Rinaldo Di Stasio and Mallory Wall 7 / 11 The restaurant had a clubby, intimate atmosphere. Courtesy Rinaldo Di Stasio and Mallory Wall 8 / 11 Rinaldo di Stasio at Cafe Di Stasio in 1990. Supplied 9 / 11 Rinaldo Di Stasio and Mallory Wall, circa 2006, in the dining room. Eamon Gallagher 10 / 11 Mallory Wall and Ronnie Di Stasio in the courtyard of Di Stasio Carlton in 2021. Kristoffer Paulsen 11 / 11 Rinaldo Di Stasio (left) with chef Valerio Nucci and Mallory Wall at Cafe Di Stasio circa 1996. Craig Abraham Previous Slide Next Slide “When we walked out at 2am on the last night two weeks ago, I was not sad,” he says. “St Kilda is not the same. The time was probably overdue for us to leave.” It was a 40-degree day on January 11, 1988, when Cafe Di Stasio opened with no air-conditioning and 45 diners for lunch. Back then, the hottest ticket in town was Lynch’s Restaurant in South Yarra, with its starched-tablecloth take on French cuisine. Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up There were great Italian restaurants in Melbourne, testaments to waves of Italian immigrants: the grand Florentino on Bourke Street and Mario’s Restaurant by the sea in Brighton. But there was nothing quite like Cafe Di Stasio.



‘The restaurant was designed for gossip, affairs, fun. Eating was just part of it.’ Rinaldo Di Stasio on Cafe Di Stasio Designed by longtime friend and collaborator, architect Allan Powell, the walls were hung with contemporary Australian art by Bill Henson, who also frequented the restaurant, and the staff wore raffish white jackets and bowties. The menu channelled an Italy that Di Stasio, born in Melbourne to Neapolitan immigrants, had soaked in during what he calls his “PhD year” living in Naples and Rome. Dishes like beef carpaccio with rocket were unfamiliar to people. Jason Lui, general manager of Flower Drum and a regular diner, describes the food as “Italian like no one else was doing it: simple and authentic”. “You went wanting to eat just a bowl of pasta,” says Lui. “But you ordered starters, dessert, champagne. You spent three times as much as you wanted to, but you left happy.” Mallory Wall (rear) briefs waiters before service at Cafe Di Stasio. Courtesy Rinaldo Di Stasio and Mallory Wall Di Stasio sums up the appeal of the restaurant as “genteel chaos”.



“There are two things people want in restaurants they don’t get at home: theatre and someone else to do the dishes. Women would sometimes say to me, ‘I could cook this at home’. I’d say, ‘No, you could cook much better, but you’d have to wash the dishes. And it wouldn’t be as fun’.” It was a hit from day one. Jill Dupleix, recipe writer, food editor and St Kilda resident at the time, went the first day for a coffee, realised it was a restaurant not a cafe, and went back for lunch, then again for dinner. “It was a pivotal restaurant for Melbourne,” she says. “It was like suddenly the grown-ups had arrived, there was a new standard in town. Ronnie cared deeply about what it was to be an Italian restaurateur and unleashed that upon the world.” Before St Kilda, Di Stasio had presided over the 500-seat, mosaic-tiled Rosati restaurant in Flinders Lane. It was the first restaurant to open on the CBD thoroughfare which has since flourished into a dining mecca. After owning the flamboyant venue for three years, Di Stasio’s relationship with his business partner imploded and he left. Ten days later, in September 1987, he signed the lease of what would become Cafe Di Stasio. “People thought I was nuts when I opened Rosati. No one paid attention to the city’s laneways. But it was one block back from Collins Street and instead of paying $3000 a week rent, I was paying $800. When I went to St Kilda, which was a pretty down-and-out suburb, people thought I was nuts again. But I cracked it.” Cafe Di Stasio in St Kilda circa 2012.



He brought with him a Rolodex of fans who filled the restaurant from lunch to dinner, along with St Kilda locals: “The artists, drag girls, the prostitutes.” “The restaurant was designed for gossip, affairs, fun. Eating was just part of it,” he says. It certainly was chaos. Two years after opening, Di Stasio was standing on the footpath outside when he spotted a woman familiar to him. She was Mallory Wall, a 21-year-old who used to wag school in Mentone to frequent Rosati, and now lived nearby after working in London for two years. He offered her a job and she started almost immediately. Her second night in the dining room was Valentine’s Day. “I looked at the bookings diary,” Wall recalls. “There were 130 people booked in. We were a 70-seat restaurant. And they were all coming at 8 o’clock.” Wall worked on bringing some order to the chaos and she and Di Stasio focused on their complementary skills in business.



“We discovered how to run a restaurant together, and discovered each other as well,” she says. Stars started swinging through the front door with its trademark bronze hands. The Rolling Stones, Nick Cave (a regular), Kevin Spacey, U2, Steve Martin, Barry Humphries, Marianne Faithfull. “It was madness. We’d push back the tables and dance in the dining room; lunch would run into dinner and then go all night,” Di Stasio says. Rinaldo Di Stasio built a reputation for long lunches and late nights at Cafe Di Stasio. Courtesy Rinaldo Di Stasio and Mallory Wall At least once a week he would jump on a table and spray the room with champagne. “It was always French, even though I tried to get him to use the cheap stuff,” says Wall. It did take a toll on Di Stasio. Seven years in, instead of opening another, larger restaurant, he bought 32-hectares in the Yarra Valley and started creating a house, designed again by Powell, and a vineyard.

World.title: I never liked small dogs. But then along came Ferdie
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsPets Opinion I never liked small dogs. But then along came Ferdie Malcolm Knox Journalist, author and columnist July 18, 2026 — 9:30am

July 18, 2026 — 9:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

This is a story about changing yourself. George Bernard Shaw said, “Those who cannot change their minds cannot change anything.” We live in a time, seemingly, of deepening entrenchment. If Shaw was right, this rigidity is not strength but powerlessness. Malcolm Knox with his dog Ferdie, a Prague ratter. I never liked small dogs. Growing up, we had medium-sized dogs, proper dogs. We had one seriously big dog: my brother, a vet who should have known his stuff, brought home a beagle pup that didn’t stop growing until he’d become a giant fox hound, who looked like Snoopy but was bigger than his kennel. Years later, my family adopted Bruce, a rescue blue heeler-kelpie cross, another proper dog with a beautiful loyal intelligence, a classic best mate. Since 2021 when he died, I was mourning Bruce. His collar still hung from the car’s rear vision mirror. Our children moved out. My beloved kept telling me I needed a dog, but I couldn’t replace Bruce (or, for that matter, the children). I didn’t replace him. Instead, I changed.



Plenty of people dislike small dogs, and I was one of them. As for very small dogs, which even the pet industry classifies as toys rather than actual dogs? Bulgy-eyed, yappy, precious little tyrants who travel in handbags: you might as well get a ferret. I didn’t want another dog anyway. Ferdie thinks I’m pretty awesome, like my kids did when they were about nine. Sometimes change comes because something deep inside you says if you don’t do it, you are giving up on more than you know. The dog change was like that. We dogsat a friend’s chihuahua, and he was unexpectedly loveable. My wife began haunting chihuahua rescue sites. A certain momentum built. Of course, it wasn’t really about a dog; it was about whether one of us had become stuck. Danger Mouse, as he was known, was having trouble getting adopted. Two years old, black with tan markings, he had behavioural problems after being raised in a family with 11 children. Yes, such families still exist, and this tiny dog had grown up with wave after wave of two-legged monsters in his face. He’d developed severe anxieties. Great. When you procrastinate for long enough, it can be best to let the universe have its way. Every good story starts with “yes”. So here I was, giving up and changing before I could get in my own way and unchange.



Because we thought he was a chihuahua, we gave him a Spanish name. Ferdie didn’t act like a chihuahua though: no barking, no aggro towards other dogs, a lusty appetite and a rather more handsome longer snout and smaller eyes offset by a weirdly big set of ears. He was also, if possible, smaller than a chihuahua. Some kind of miniature pinscher? Then during a morning walk, this random woman said, “Is that a Prague ratter?” Excuse me, we don’t think so. Did she just call our dog a rat? On a city walk, a young drinker in a pub yelled out, “Oi, how’s ya Prague ratter!” What the actual? An imposter chihuahua? We looked up Prague ratters and they looked like Ferdie. The behavioural tics – the non-barking, the ease around other dogs, the food obsession, the devotion to curling up in your lap – were pure Prague ratter. There aren’t many in Australia and only Ferdie knows how he got here, but he’s telling no tales. Conveniently, Ferdinand can also be a Central European name. The best thing about toy dogs, what I never realised because I never liked them, is how much pleasure they give strangers. Honestly, it’s like walking around with Timothée Chalamet on a leash. The guy’s a superstar. Kids, adults, old folk, it doesn’t matter: Ferdie puts smiles on faces. You can’t go one block without being stopped by people who want to pat him, talk to him, ask you about him. Passers-by say, “Look, he’s so cute!” and they’re not talking about me. As charismatic as Bruce was, he was a D-list celebrity compared with this bloke. It’s nice to make people happy without doing anything to earn it.



Related Article Pets After three days on a ledge, and two at the vet, Elbie is just fine. For her owner, it’s a different story He’s become the most photographed member of the family. Beyond cuteness, why does a dog complete the picture? In a new book about dogs in art, The Dog’s Gaze, historian Thomas Laqueur details how the first family member Odysseus meets, returning to Ithaca in Homer’s Odyssey, is his dog Argos: “Look! – he wagged his tail and both his ears went flat.” Centuries later, the photographer Richard Avedon said his parents always borrowed a dog for family portraits. “They bring their world into ours, which is perhaps how they make us feel less lonely as a species,” Laqueur writes. “They humanise humans.” Ferdie is gracious about his work to humanise humans. Like a Sam Neill of dogs, he takes it in his stride and is happy to have made others happy. You wouldn’t call him gregarious, and he’s actually hoping they have food for him, but he has none of that small-dog Napoleon syndrome. He gets on with fellow dogs except the odd greyhound who eyes him off like he’s an hors d’oeuvre. Out in the world, he’s a lover, not a fighter. Different story at home, where he seems to think that I need a bodyguard. In a recent American YouGov survey, 95 per cent of dog owners said their pet gave them unconditional love. Ferdie thinks I’m pretty awesome, like my kids did when they were about nine, but he also thinks I need close protection. He thinks any visitor has come to hurt or steal me. He has bitten my brother, my son, my daughter, my friends, my mother-in-law, the neighbours and the oven man. Visitors/intruders/hostile alien life-forms need to pass this trial before he settles down. Prague ratters don’t take well to types of discipline that work for other dogs: we tried using a water spray to correct his behaviour and he nearly took our arm off. As a last resort, there are muzzles small enough to fit over one of your fingers. Nobody’s perfect. He hates being left alone but at least he doesn’t take it out on the furniture. He’s more or less house-trained but isn’t above the occasional excitement wee or poo; he just prefers to do his ablutions out on the Walk of Fame.



In that same YouGov survey, 66 per cent of owners thought their dogs’ intelligence was above-average and 27 per cent average, leaving just 7 per cent who thought their dogs were below average. Everyone scores an A. I’ll admit Ferdie is probably among the 7 per cent. What is dog intelligence worth anyway, when you put so many smiles on faces? Having changed, there was one other change to cope with. Chihuahuas’ life expectancy can be 20-plus years, whereas Prague ratters only live to 12 or so. So we probably won’t have him as long as expected. More reason to make the most of things while they last. By that time, I’ll have become that most risible of human beings, the “toy-dog person”. I might have reckoned with other new realities. If you can change not only your views but your affinities, not only your likes but your loves, not only your preferences but your weaknesses, then you can still change the world beyond your door. Malcolm Knox is a journalist, author and columnist. The Opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here

World.title: From garbo to Italian job: Paenga-Amosa’s lesson in resilience for struggling Wallabies
World.content:
SportRugby UnionWallabies From garbo to Italian job: Paenga-Amosa’s lesson in resilience for struggling Wallabies Jonathan Drennan July 18, 2026 — 9:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

After nine losses in their past 10 Test matches, the Wallabies are being forced to learn about resilience. Hooker Brandon Paenga-Amosa is well qualified to be their teacher. Before turning professional, he taught a class in mental strength to teenagers in western Sydney and would wake up at 4am to work as a garbage man across Redfern in the depths of winter. Brandon Paenga-Amosa of the Wallabies celebrates scoring a try earlier in the game. Getty Images That background gives Paenga-Amosa a different mindset than most heading into Saturday’s clash with Italy in Perth. “It’s just perspective ahead of this game. I could be digging holes out the back. I could be running behind the garbage truck getting a bit of bin juice on me here and there,” Paenga-Amosa said.



“Those jobs definitely shaped my perspective on the world and just life in general. But with that being said, I wouldn’t change anything about the route that I took. “Even as a dad, to be able to teach my kids that sometimes what you want takes a bit of work.” Brandon-Paenga Amosa acknowledging the work of teammate Angus Bell Getty Images Paenga-Amosa was never picked for representative sides as a schoolboy and worked as a garbage man, a teacher, a gardener, a trampoline attendant and a labourer while playing for Southern Districts in the Shute Shield. His shot at professional rugby came in 2018 at the Reds. He spent three years in Brisbane and then three seasons in France with Montpellier before returning to Australia to play for the Western Force.



In the Wallabies’ defeat against France last Saturday, Paenga-Amosa was outstanding, coming off the bench after three minutes and finishing the game after Josh Nasser was ruled out after a head knock. He playfully sledged the French front row in their native language during the scrum and after scoring a try, but got tongue-tied as fatigue set in. Even in the dark moments that come when plying your trade as a Test hooker, Paenga-Amosa regularly pops up from scrums and mauls with a wide smile on his face. The Western Force player always wants to show his appreciation for his teammates during the toughest of times on the field. “I always look at the cup half-full rather than half-empty; I love getting around the boys, and I love big moments in games,” Paenga-Amosa said. “When we win those moments, like a scrum penalty or a try, there aren’t many things in the world that can beat that feeling. “For me, rugby’s more than just the game ... There’s a strong brotherhood in the squad, and honestly these last two losses [against France and Ireland] have actually brought us together even closer as a team, which is important.”



Related Article Wallabies Wallabies’ playmaker carousel spins on as Cooper questions Lolesio snub Against Italy, Paenga-Amosa will face a squad full of confidence after a strong Six Nations campaign, but he believes a win for the Wallabies will create momentum that is desperately needed ahead of new coach Les Kiss taking over. “Once we get that one win, it’ll snowball into more wins. We deserve it, I feel we beat ourselves in the last two games,” Paenga-Amosa said. “It would be really good for us as a squad to not beat ourselves in this next game, to actually earn the win that we deserve and put together a performance that not just we’re proud of, but our supporters, our country and our nation are proud of as well.”

World.title: If the hapless ’Tahs are putting the 2014 band back together, don’t stop at Foley and Phipps
World.content:
SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby Opinion If the hapless ’Tahs are putting the 2014 band back together, don’t stop at Foley and Phipps Iain Payten Senior Sports Reporter July 18, 2026 — 10:52am

July 18, 2026 — 10:52am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

News that Bernard Foley and Nick Phipps are returning to the Waratahs next season produced predictable responses this week. The next signing has to be Cliffy Palu. Bring back Jacques Potgieter. Where is Jeremy Tilse? Loading Pick a member of the Waratahs’ title-winning squad in 2014 and their name has appeared in the comments this week. Given Foley and Phipps were both stars of that side, and are on the downhill slope to 40, it was an understandable reflex from the rugby world. But those fans with sky-blue blood had another understandable response: what the hell do these signings say about pathways and talent development inside the Rugby Australia-owned Waratahs?



The rage is justified and slightly misplaced. Signing the duo is decent business given the circumstances, but how the Waratahs and RA got themselves into this position is bush league stuff. Phipps has come in as an 11th-hour filler, following a last-round injury to Jake Gordon that’ll sideline him for the first third of 2027, and a decision to let Michael McDonald go as the third halfback on the roster. Rumours that Teddy Wilson is leaving are wrong, he has re-signed for next season. The Waratahs celebrate after beating the Crusaders in the 2014 Super Rugby final. Mark Nolan/Getty Images Under the terms of his contract, the Tahs have 19-year-old halfback Angus Grover progressing from the academy into the main squad in 2027, and though he’s a very promising Junior Wallaby, it’s too early in his career for the physicality of Super Rugby. That risk was exposed by Gordon’s injury. Hence Phipps. Foley’s return follows two other roster moves at No.10.



Impressed by his Super Rugby AU form for the Force, then-Waratahs coach Dan McKellar signed Max Burey in January for 2027 and via his contract, rising Sydney University No.10 Joey Fowler was also promoted from the academy to the main squad for 2027. Fowler, 21, was the Junior Wallabies five-eighth for the previous two campaigns. Burey, 27, is a Tahs junior and Norths utility who has played 37 Super Rugby games over four seasons at the Force, primarily off the bench. Bernard Foley kicking a conversion for Kubota. Getty That left just one five-eighth slot left at the Tahs, and with Jack Debreczeni retiring, Foley was targeted by McKellar as an experienced playmaker to both play and mentor. The problem? That has left no room for Jack Bowen, a 22-year-old who’d spent four seasons at the Tahs but was given little opportunity. He played 17 games and started five, all at the end of seasons. Mostly, Bowen did well with those chances, and he finished as the Tahs’ starting No.10 this year.



The Easts pivot has also been the standout five-eighth in the Shute Shield for several seasons. But, on Friday, Bowen was released and farewelled by the Waratahs. He is looking at overseas options. Young playmaker Jack Bowen has been cut by the Waratahs. Getty Images Somehow the Waratahs have again pushed out a homegrown NSW five-eighth, after years of development and investment. But amazingly, Bowen is the latest in a long list. In 2023, the Waratahs had Will Harrison, Ben Donaldson, Tane Edmed and Bowen on the books. Four years later, all are gone.



Each case has its own story, but the negligence of the Waratahs in letting NSW playmakers in their early 20s depart is a constant theme. It is time the bleeding stopped - and that can start by correcting the Bowen decision, to make sure his NSW-funded development is not enjoyed by a French or Japanese club for the next three years. Michael Cheika and Michael Hooper celebrate victory over the Crusaders in the Super Rugby decider in 2014. Getty With Foley on a one-season deal, the Tahs will have a big gap again in 2028 and by early next year they’ll be looking for a NSW pivot with professional experience, or at least Shute Shield dominance. They’ve got both in Bowen, and the Waratahs can head off the criticism coming their way with Foley’s return by going back to Bowen and working out a deal for 2028. The other pride-swallowing step the Waratahs - read Rugby Australia - should take is to pick up the phone and talk turkey with one more 2014 alumni: coach Michael Cheika.



It defies belief that RA are not in discussions with Cheika about the possibility of him taking over the vacancy left by McKellar last month. Cheika is a thoroughbred gift-horse for RA. You’d struggle to find anyone who doesn’t believe Cheika would turn the Waratahs around. He has made a career of it. Cheika’s CV will be many miles better than any of the candidates RA will gather in their search. There is a reason why Test nations and major clubs hammer his phone regularly. Influential Waratahs players are even pushing internally for Cheika. For whatever reason, risk-averse types at RA are reluctant to consider the Cheika package, which is viewed as unmanageable and not “aligned” to the steady, process-driven ethos of RA’s top brass.



Related Article Wallabies Wallabies’ playmaker carousel spins on as Cooper questions Lolesio snub Much of that stuff is stereotyped. Cheika is not the hot-headed wild man of yesteryear. He would insist on being the boss at the Waratahs, for sure, but that’s exactly what is needed. On their trajectory, the Waratahs are getting close to falling off the sporting map in NSW. Seeing stands full for Wallabies games in Sydney should be more of a source of pain for RA than back-slapping, knowing three-quarters of those same rugby fans are not interested in watching the Waratahs. RA have spent huge sums on the poster-boy stars at NSW - Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii, Max Jorgensen, the incoming NRL recruit Angus Crichton - but without success, the Waratahs won’t be a hot ticket and the investment wasted. Cheika is a no-brainer as the best option to bring back success and re-engage an apathetic public. Frame it with a succession plan, if the jitters feel too strong. Install Stephen Hoiles or Chris Latham as an assistant, and set up a handover in two years’ time. There is a reason people remember Phipps and Foley, and make 2014 jokes. That was the last time the state was truly invested in the Waratahs.

World.title: War between US and Iran expands as bridges and water plant hit, more ships attacked
World.content:
WorldMiddle EastMiddle East at war War between US and Iran expands as bridges and water plant hit, more ships attacked Jana Choukeir and Enas Alashray July 18, 2026 — 10:33am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Dubai/Cairo: The US struck bridges in Iran, and Tehran responded by hitting a power and desalination plant in Kuwait, as the two sides risked further escalation by expanding their targets to include infrastructure. At sea, where the renewed conflict has again cut off energy supplies from the Gulf, US Marines boarded a tanker near the Strait of Hormuz. Loading Two oil tankers exploded and caught fire after passing through a mined route south of the strait, Iranian media reported, citing Iran’s Revolutionary Guards. The US military denied that, saying, “Like most IRGC claims, this is false.” Armed men seized another vessel off Yemen, raising concern over security in the Middle East’s other big choke point for oil shipments at the mouth of the Red Sea.



Iran’s state television quoted the Revolutionary Guards as saying that until US “aggression” comes to an end, it will not be possible to export chemical fertilisers or even a “single drop of oil and gas” from the region. Washington and Tehran have been testing the limits of escalation since their ceasefire agreement collapsed last week, raising the prospect of a return to all-out war. Pro-government demonstrators gather at a square in Tehran on Friday. AP Photo/Vahid Salemi After reports of the escalation on Friday (US time), benchmark Brent crude oil prices climbed 3 per cent and were on track for a third consecutive weekly gain, putting political pressure on US President Donald Trump ahead of November congressional elections. Trump has threatened to launch broad-based air strikes on Iran’s infrastructure and has also declined to rule out a ground assault on Iran’s coast or islands. US officials have said attacks on southern Iran are designed in part to give Trump options.



Such moves risk provoking Iran to escalate in turn by hitting the vital infrastructure of vulnerable Gulf states, or having its allies in Yemen further disrupt global energy supplies by attacking shipping from the Red Sea. Mohsen Rezaei, an adviser to Iran’s supreme leader, warned on Friday against US escalation or any attempt to seize Iranian territory. US President Donald Trump in New York on Friday. AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin “If US strikes continue for several more days, we will move into a phase of full-scale offensive operations,” Rezaei, a former Revolutionary Guards top commander, told state television. United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres was concerned about the escalation, particularly “attacks on civilian infrastructure in Iran and across the region”, his spokesperson said.



The US military’s Central Command earlier said its targets included “military logistics infrastructure”, the first time it mentioned infrastructure in more than a week. In the latest strikes, Central Command said it reinitiated attacks on Iran for the seventh consecutive night, with strikes about 5am on Saturday (AEST), around 10.30pm on Friday in Tehran. View post on X “The strikes are designed to continue degrading Iranian military capabilities at the Commander in Chief’s direction,” the statement on X said. Shortly thereafter, Iranian media reported explosions were heard or strikes carried out in Sirik, Ahvaz and Yazd. Iran’s semi-official Mehr news agency said no casualties were reported from enemy projectiles outside Yazd, a central city about 600 kilometres south of Tehran.



Iranian state media previously said at least five bridges were struck in the south. Seven people were reported killed in attacks on bridges in the southern port of Bandar Khamir, where the train station was also hit. An airport was reported hit further east and away from the coast in Iranshahr, in a province bordering Pakistan. Videos verified by Reuters showed rubble, broken railings and a damaged vehicle on a smashed bridge in Bandar Khamir. One clip showed a fire. Iran announced attacks on Gulf countries that host US airbases, including Bahrain, Qatar and Kuwait, in addition to a US vessel in the northern Indian Ocean. The Revolutionary Guards said it attacked a depot of US drones in Bahrain and destroyed Bahrain’s main artificial intelligence centre with ballistic missiles and drones. The Iranian navy fired a shore-to-sea cruise missile towards what it called a hostile US vessel in the northern Indian Ocean, state news agency IRNA reported on Friday. Iran’s army said the missile launch caused “fear and panic” and forced the vessel to move out of range of Iran’s navy.



Authorities in Kuwait said one of the country’s power generation and water desalination stations had been hit in an Iranian attack, causing damage, a fire, and the disruption of many electricity generation units. Related Article Middle East at war Trump sets sights on Iran’s hidden nuclear fortress The rich Arab Gulf states depend on plants that produce electricity and remove salt from seawater to make their desert cities habitable. When Iran hit a Kuwaiti desalination plant on March 30, it was seen as a major escalation. Last month’s interim agreement to end the war has collapsed since July 7, when Iran struck ships in the Strait of Hormuz and the United States responded with air strikes. Iran has since announced the closure of the strait, and Washington has reimposed its own blockade of Iranian ports. World.title: ‘He’s not a cheater’: DeChambeau to continue playing at British Open as controversy erupts over two-shot penalty
World.content:
Updated SportGolfBritish Open ‘He’s not a cheater’: DeChambeau to continue playing at British Open as controversy erupts over two-shot penalty Tom Decent Updated July 18, 2026 — 10:13am ,first published July 18, 2026 — 8:07am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Southport: Controversy has erupted at the British Open, with American star Bryson DeChambeau set to continue his campaign after initially threatening to withdraw from the tournament when he was controversially docked two shots by officials on Friday. DeChambeau was hit with a two-shot penalty for “improving the area” of his intended back swing during his second round, prompting his agent to declare his client wasn’t a cheat and he wasn’t trying to gain an unfair advantage during an incident that has divided the golf world. Bryson DeChambeau speaks with officials after his round on Friday at the British Open. X After carding a four-under 66 on Friday, DeChambeau walked off the 18th green at Royal Birkdale in outright second on seven-under, behind Australia’s Lucas Herbert, who shot a record-equalling 62 to head to the weekend at eight-under. But after signing his card, DeChambeau was approached by rules officials over an incident on the fifth hole earlier in the day.



Playing his second shot from thick rough, television footage appeared to show DeChambeau walking around the area of his ball before taking his shot, with officials believing his actions improved the area where his club would swing. Although the ball itself never moved, the rules of golf prohibit players from improving the area of an intended stance or swing, even if the action is accidental. DeChambeau and his agent Brett Falkoff (left) on a controversial evening at the British Open. Getty Images A frustrated DeChambeau was taken back to the fifth hole by officials, where he remonstrated with tournament staff and appeared to tell decision-makers he would not continue in the championship. His manager was also present during the dramatic exchange broadcast on live television. Shortly afterwards, amid a crush of television cameras and reporters, tournament rules official Grant Moir confirmed DeChambeau had been docked two shots. His bogey on the 5th hole would become a triple bogey seven.



The penalty dropped DeChambeau from seven-under to five-under, leaving him tied for fifth rather than second. “Bryson has been penalised two strokes for inadvertently improving the area of intended back swing on fifth hole,” Moir said. Grant Moir, executive director of governance at The R&A, speaks to the media regarding a two-stoke penalty assessed against DeChambeau. Getty Images “Ruling one restricts what a player may do to improve any of the protected conditions affecting the stroke and this includes the area of the player’s intended swing. “So an improvement means to alter one or more of the conditions affecting the stroke so that the player gains a potential advantage for the stroke. Now, I’ll stress that this applies even when the action is accidental, as it was in Bryson’s case.”



When asked by reporters as he walked away whether he would return for Saturday’s third round, DeChambeau stopped short of giving any assurance. DeChambeau’s agent Brett Falkoff also said he would decide on Saturday morning whether he would continue playing but said his 32-year-old client is angry. However, at 12.02am UK time, DeChambeau wrote on X: “Obviously disappointed with the ruling. I don’t agree with it, but it is what it is. This fires me up. Onto the weekend. Let’s get it.” Earlier, DeChambeau headed to the practice range after being informed of his penalty, where he began hitting balls as darkness fell over Royal Birkdale. “He’s a lot of things. He’s not a cheater,” Falkoff said. “He’s a big boy … but he certainly feels he was unfairly penalised.”



Related Article British Open Herbert stuns with record-equalling round at British Open, but final putt could haunt him forever DeChambeau is a popular player on tour but also divisive among fans, having defected to LIV Golf on a lucrative deal worth more than $100 million (USD). Herbert was supposed to be paired with DeChambeau on Saturday but the latest drama means he will instead play his third round with Jackson Suber at 3.50pm local time (12.50am AEST). DeChambeau, a two-time US Open champion, is listed to tee off at 3.30pm (12.30am). He has never won a British Open. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.
